rw1.passage: Seeking to the spread of an invasive beetle, forestry officials restricted the movement of firewood between counties, since the insects often travel hidden inside cut logs.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw1.why: The colon explains that the menu has only five dishes, so limited is the logical word. Sprawling is the opposite, and the passage says nothing about indifference or age.
rw1.passage: The chef's menu is deliberately : it lists only five dishes, each built from ingredients grown within a few miles of the restaurant.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw1.why: She repeats herself to avoid disappointing buyers, which shows a reluctance to take risks that complacent captures. Curious would lead her to experiment, and nothing suggests generosity or impatience.
rw1.passage: Though her early paintings were widely admired, the artist found that success had made her ; she began to repeat herself, afraid of disappointing buyers who expected the same bright landscapes.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw1.why: Dense shade that blocks seedlings suggests very large, dominant trees, and imposing conveys that. Delicate and unremarkable would not cast such shade.
rw1.passage: The oldest trees in the grove are so that foresters have not found any seedlings growing within thirty metres of them; their dense shade prevents young trees from taking root.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw1.why: The underlined sentence says what the angle and duration of the dance mean, which explains how the dance carries information. It does not question bee communication or compare other insects.
rw1.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original science article.

Honeybees communicate the location of food through a pattern of movement known as the waggle dance. The angle of the bee's run relative to vertical corresponds to the direction of the food relative to the sun, while the duration of the waggle signals the distance. Other bees in the hive follow the dancer, then fly out to search the indicated area.
rw1.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It questions whether bees can communicate with one another.
It compares the dance with the way other insects find food.
It explains how the features of the dance convey information about the food.
It describes what happens when bees fail to find food.

rw1.why: Lucía sets everything back where it was and cannot turn the calendar page, which shows her reluctance to disturb her aunt's life. She is careful, not careless, and the text does not explain the tidiness or suggest haste.
rw1.passage:
The following text is from an original short story. Lucía has come to collect her late aunt's belongings.

The flat smelled of lemon polish and old paper. Lucía moved from room to room with a box she did not fill, lifting a teacup, a scarf, a folded letter, and setting each one down again exactly where it had been. It seemed impossible to rearrange a life that had been so precisely arranged. In the kitchen, a calendar still showed the month of her aunt's last week, a dentist's appointment circled in red; Lucía found she could not turn the page.
rw1.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe the carelessness with which Lucía treats her aunt's things
To explain why Lucía's aunt kept the flat so tidy
To suggest that Lucía is hurrying to finish an unpleasant task
To show Lucía's reluctance to disturb the traces of her aunt's life

rw1.why: The text says the harvests are modest and that the real yield is social. It denies that the gardens could feed a neighbourhood and says nothing about difficulty or about most residents.
rw1.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original essay about urban gardening.

On rooftops across the city, residents have begun growing tomatoes, beans and herbs in raised beds. The harvests are modest and will never feed a neighbourhood. But those who garden say the real yield is something else: the conversations over the fence, the sharing of seeds, the sense of belonging to a place they might otherwise only pass through.
rw1.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Rooftop gardens can supply enough food for an entire neighbourhood.
Growing tomatoes is more difficult in a city than in the countryside.
Rooftop gardens are valued by their keepers less for the food they produce than for the community they create.
Most city residents have taken up gardening in recent years.

rw1.why: The text says the viaduct's failure is what she is remembered for, but that a contractor swapped her steel for a cheaper alloy. Nothing is said about destroyed notebooks, dismissing vibration, or being first to use steel.
rw1.passage:
The following text is from an original essay about a historical figure.

The engineer Rosalind Teague is remembered, if at all, for a single failure: a viaduct that closed after only six years. Yet her notebooks show a designer far ahead of her time, one who calculated the effects of vibration decades before it became standard practice. The viaduct failed in part because the contractor replaced her specified steel with a cheaper alloy; her calculations, applied correctly, would have kept it standing.
rw1.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Teague's notebooks were destroyed after the viaduct closed.
Teague argued that vibration should never be considered in bridge design.
Teague was the first engineer to use steel in a viaduct.
Teague's reputation rests on a failure that was caused largely by decisions made against her design.

rw1.why: The sparseness of the later music is shown by the work asking the orchestra to play almost nothing. The first quotation describes the early dense style, and the others are either not about sparseness or describe its effect.
rw1.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original essay about a composer.

In her early symphonies, the composer Anneli Vos filled every bar with sound, layering strings over brass over percussion. Her last works could hardly be more different. One of them asks the orchestra to play almost nothing for nearly a minute, leaving the audience with only the faint creak of seats.
rw1.q: A student claims that Vos's later music is much sparser than her earlier music. Which quotation from the text best supports the student's claim?
choices: "filled every bar with sound, layering strings over brass over percussion"
"leaving the audience with only the faint creak of seats"
"One of them asks the orchestra to play almost nothing for nearly a minute"

rw1.why: Pages folded and stitched around the cover show the fragment was used to bind the ledger. The language, the contents of the ledger and other holdings do not address how the fragment was used.
rw1.passage:
A student is writing about the discovery of a medieval manuscript.

In 2018, a cataloguer at a regional archive found that a bundle of accounts, long assumed to be a farm's ledger, contained a fragment of a twelfth-century poem on its back pages. The fragment had been used as scrap to bind the ledger, a common practice at the time.
rw1.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the claim that the fragment was reused as binding material rather than copied into the ledger?
choices: The poem is written in a language no longer spoken.
The ledger lists the sale of livestock.
Its pages were folded and stitched around the ledger's cover.
The archive holds other twelfth-century manuscripts.

rw1.why: Seeds that germinate in response to smoke are adapted to take advantage of conditions after fires. The text does not say they cannot grow elsewhere, and it contradicts the other choices.
rw1.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original science article.

Seeds of the fire poppy can lie dormant in soil for decades without sprouting. Researchers studying burned hillsides noticed that the flowers appeared in large numbers only after wildfires, and they found that chemicals in smoke trigger germination. This suggests that fire poppies
rw1.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: are adapted to take advantage of conditions created by fire.
are unable to grow in any soil that has not burned.
sprout every year regardless of the conditions.
produce seeds that are harmed by smoke.

rw1.why: The researcher notes the cause might run the other way, so the survey alone cannot show that reading builds vocabulary. It does not show harm, claim that weak readers never read, or restrict the findings to one university.
rw1.passage:
The following text is from an original essay about reading habits.

A survey of university students found that those who read for pleasure at least an hour a week scored higher on a test of vocabulary than those who did not. The researcher cautions, however, that students with strong vocabularies may simply find reading more enjoyable and so do more of it. The survey's results therefore
rw1.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: prove that reading for pleasure harms vocabulary.
do not show by themselves that reading for pleasure improves vocabulary.
show that students with weak vocabularies never read.
apply only to students at one university.

rw1.passage: The students in Ms. Alvarez's class their projects on local history to the school board next week.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

rw1.why: The three items form a parallel list of plural nouns, so textiles is correct. The other choices break the parallel structure.
rw1.passage: The museum's collection includes paintings, sculptures, and from every continent.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

rw1.passage: Having studied the migration of monarch butterflies for a decade,
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Dr. Kim presented her findings at the annual meeting.
her findings were presented by Dr. Kim at the annual meeting.
the annual meeting heard Dr. Kim's findings.
it was Dr. Kim who presented findings at the meeting.

rw1.passage: The new bridge, which took nearly four years to build finally opened to traffic in March.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

rw1.why: The subject each is singular, so the verb is receives. The other choices are plural or ungrammatical.
rw1.passage: Each of the volunteers a badge at the entrance.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

rw1.why: The semicolon joins two independent clauses, and the second is a result of the first, so as a result is correct.
rw1.passage: Maya studied hard for the exam; she earned the highest score in her class.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

rw1.why: The second clause gives the reason the discovery was important, so because is the logical conjunction.
rw1.passage: The scientist's discovery was important it changed how researchers thought about the origins of the disease.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

rw1.why: The botanical classification contrasts with the culinary one, so however is the right transition.
rw1.passage: Tomatoes are usually classed as vegetables because they are served with savoury food. Botanically, they are fruit, since they develop from the flower's ovary and contain seeds.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

rw1.why: The fall in commuting times confirms what was expected, so Indeed is the logical transition.
rw1.passage: The city's new bike lanes were expected to reduce traffic. commuting times have fallen by an average of five minutes since they opened.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

rw1.why: The sentence corrects the earlier belief with a fact, so In fact is the best transition. Likewise suggests similarity, and the others do not fit.
rw1.passage: Biologists once thought that all bats find their way by echolocation. some fruit bats, which rely mainly on sight and smell, do not use it at all.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

rw1.why: To explain what the building is for, the choice must state its function, and only the first mentions tracking variable stars. The others give its history, visiting hours or an installation date.
rw1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Merrow Observatory stands on a hill above the town of Kell.
  • It was built in 1912.
  • Its main instrument is a 40-centimetre refracting telescope.
  • The telescope is used to track variable stars.
  • The observatory is open to the public on clear Friday evenings.

The student wants to explain what a particular building is for.
rw1.q: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: The Merrow Observatory, built in 1912, stands on a hill above the town of Kell.
The Merrow Observatory is open to the public on clear Friday evenings.
A telescope was installed at the observatory when it was built in 1912.
The Merrow Observatory above Kell uses a 40-centimetre refracting telescope to track variable stars.

rw1.why: A comparison needs details about both rivers on the same points, which the first choice gives. The others describe one river or the shared sea.
rw1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Orla River is 480 kilometres long.
  • The Tamsin River is 310 kilometres long.
  • The Orla flows through three countries.
  • The Tamsin flows through one country.
  • Both rivers empty into the same sea.

The student wants to make a comparison between two rivers.
rw1.q: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: The Orla River, which is 480 kilometres long, flows through three countries.
Both the Orla and the Tamsin rivers empty into the same sea.
The Orla River is 480 kilometres long and passes through three countries, while the Tamsin is 310 kilometres long and stays within one.
The Tamsin River is 310 kilometres long and flows through only one country.

rw1.why: Age is conveyed by the date of around 1190, which only the first choice gives. The others describe the codex's contents, material or restoration.
rw1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Tarn Codex is held in a library in Lisbon.
  • It is written on parchment.
  • Scholars date it to around the year 1190.
  • It contains 120 pages of astronomical tables.
  • It was restored in 1985.

The student wants to emphasise the age of a manuscript.
rw1.q: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Scholars date the Tarn Codex, which is held in a library in Lisbon, to around the year 1190.
The Tarn Codex, restored in 1985, contains 120 pages of astronomical tables.
The Tarn Codex is written on parchment and held in a library in Lisbon.
The Tarn Codex contains astronomical tables on 120 pages of parchment.

rw2h.why: She said enough to be friendly but nothing binding, so her remarks were carefully measured. Calibrated fits. Impulsive and defiant contradict the care described, and garbled would mean confused.
rw2h.passage: The ambassador's remarks were carefully : she affirmed her country's friendship with its neighbour while avoiding any statement that might later be read as a commitment.
rw2h.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw2h.why: The sentence describes a disease once confined to the tropics, so scourge, meaning a source of affliction, is the fitting noun. Haven and remedy suggest benefit, and relic implies something from the past.
rw2h.passage: Once regarded as a of the tropics, the disease has been spreading northward as warming temperatures allow its mosquito carriers to survive in regions that were formerly too cold.
rw2h.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw2h.why: Wording that lets both sides claim a win must be capable of several readings, which elastic suggests. Rigid and emphatic would leave little room for dispute.
rw2h.passage: The treaty's language was so that each side could claim it had won a concession, a flexibility that smoothed the signing but sowed disputes for years afterward.
rw2h.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw2h.why: Far from signals that she was the opposite of resistant, and she actively sought criticism. Impervious means unable to be affected, which fits the contrast. Vulnerable and sensitive would not contrast with seeking criticism.
rw2h.passage: Far from being to criticism, the physicist actively sought it, circulating drafts of her papers to rivals and asking them to find flaws before publication.
rw2h.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw2h.why: The underlined sentence describes the slow accumulation of discrepancies, which shows that the revolution was gradual, contrary to the popular image of one decisive moment. It does not describe a single experiment, say the old model had no defenders, or introduce a theory to be evaluated.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original essay about the history of science.

We tend to imagine that a scientific revolution arrives with a single experiment, a decisive moment. But the shift in astronomy that replaced the earth-centred view of the cosmos unfolded over more than a century. Observers had to accumulate small discrepancies, one by one, until the old model required so many patches that its defenders themselves began to doubt it. Only then did the new view appear not as heresy but as relief.
rw2h.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It describes a single experiment that settled a long-running dispute.
It argues that the old model was never defended by astronomers.
It explains how the slow accumulation of evidence, rather than one decisive moment, brought about the change.
It introduces a new theory that the passage goes on to evaluate.

rw2h.why: The sentence lists real hazards the speeches ignored, which supports Corliss's impression that the speakers lack knowledge of the sea. It does not mention a speech by him, claim the vessel is more dangerous, or say the harbour is now safe.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is from an original novel. Corliss is a retired ferry captain who has been invited to the christening of a new vessel.

Corliss stood at the back of the crowd, his good coat buttoned against a wind he could have told them about. The speeches praised the vessel's engines, its modern radar, its capacity for four hundred passengers. Nobody mentioned the harbour mouth, where the current doubled back on itself after the turn of the tide, or the shoal that had taken three boats in his time. He had the odd impression of attending the christening of a ship by people who had never been to sea.
rw2h.q: Which choice best describes the function of the sentence beginning "Nobody mentioned the harbour mouth" in the text as a whole?
choices: It shows that Corliss has been asked to give a speech.
It reveals that the vessel is more dangerous than earlier ones.
It contrasts the harbour's present safety with its past dangers.
It illustrates what Corliss feels the speakers have overlooked.

rw2h.why: Text 2 notes the new styles began before photography spread, so the historian would say Text 1 mistakes cause for coincidence or acceleration. The historian says the camera made visible an existing interest, so does not deny all influence.
rw2h.passage:
Text 1

Some art historians argue that the invention of photography freed painters from the duty to depict the world accurately. With the camera available to record a likeness, they say, painters were able to explore colour and form for their own sake, a development that led to the movements of the late nineteenth century.

Text 2

A historian of technology notes that the new painting styles were already emerging before photography became widespread. She argues that the camera did not cause painters to abandon realism so much as make visible an interest in perception that many of them already had.
rw2h.q: Based on the texts, how would the historian in Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that painters lost interest in realism only after the camera appeared
By arguing that photography had no influence on painters at all
By claiming that painters' new styles were invented by photographers
By suggesting that the claim wrongly treats photography as the cause of changes that were already under way

rw2h.why: The text reports membraneless droplets that act as compartments, which means cells need less physical structure than thought. It says the picture is more crowded, not less, and oil is only an analogy.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original science article.

The common view of cells as bags of chemicals floating in fluid has given way to a more crowded picture. Using new microscopes, researchers have found that many cellular reactions occur not in open solution but within droplets that form and dissolve like oil in water, concentrating the molecules that need to meet. These droplets lack membranes, yet they behave as distinct compartments, suggesting that cells organise their chemistry with far less physical structure than had been believed necessary.
rw2h.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Cells are less crowded than researchers once believed.
Recent observations indicate that cells can organise chemical reactions in compartments that have no membranes.
Droplets in cells form only when oil is present.
New microscopes have made membranes unnecessary for cells.

rw2h.why: The text argues that GDP counts all spending, including repair of damage, so it should not be read as welfare. It does not say GDP falls with repairs, or that economists have abandoned it.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original essay about economics.

It is tempting to treat a country's gross domestic product as a measure of well-being, but the figure counts any spending as a gain. Money spent cleaning up an oil spill raises GDP; so does money spent on medicine for an illness caused by pollution. An economist who reads the figure as a measure of welfare must therefore explain why a society that has to spend more to repair damage should count itself better off.
rw2h.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: GDP is a poor measure of well-being because it counts spending that merely repairs harm as a gain.
GDP falls whenever a society spends money on repairs.
Economists have abandoned GDP as a measure of national income.
Spending on medicine is the main source of economic growth.

By week 12, plants given the higher amount had grown to 92 centimetres, about 30 centimetres taller than plants given the lower amount.
By week 12, plants given the lower amount had grown to 92 centimetres, about 15 centimetres taller than plants given the higher amount.
By week 8, plants given the higher amount had grown to 92 centimetres, about 15 centimetres taller than plants given the lower amount.

rw2h.why: The claim is that a mistaken theory could still lead to effective remedies, and only the quotation saying the measures worked but not for the believed reason states this directly. The others describe the theory, the measures or one mechanism without making the point.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original essay on the history of medicine.

Before germ theory, physicians commonly attributed fevers to bad air, and their remedies were aimed at purifying it: burning herbs, opening windows, relocating patients to hills. These measures sometimes worked, though not for the reason physicians believed; moving a sick person out of a crowded ward also reduced the chance of spreading infection to others.
rw2h.q: A student claims that remedies based on a mistaken theory could still be effective. Which quotation from the text best supports the student's claim?
choices: "Before germ theory, physicians commonly attributed fevers to bad air"
"burning herbs, opening windows, relocating patients to hills"
"moving a sick person out of a crowded ward also reduced the chance of spreading infection"
"These measures sometimes worked, though not for the reason physicians believed"

rw2h.why: Forest birds raising their pitch after exposure to traffic noise shows that noise itself can produce the change, which supports the researcher's causal claim. The other choices say nothing about noise causing a pitch change.
rw2h.passage:
A researcher claims that urban birds sing at a higher pitch than rural birds of the same species because lower notes are masked by traffic noise.

In a study of great tits, the average song pitch was found to be 12 percent higher in a noisy city than in a quiet forest. When researchers played recordings of traffic to forest birds, the birds raised their pitch within a few days.
rw2h.q: Which finding from the text most directly supports the researcher's claim about the cause of the higher pitch?
choices: City birds sing more often than forest birds.
Forest birds raised their pitch after being exposed to recordings of traffic.
The study was carried out on great tits.
Great tits are common in both cities and forests.

rw2h.why: Narrow, winding streets inside walls contrasted with wider ones built once the threat lessened, which suggests the earlier layout reflected defensive needs. Speed and shared architects are not suggested, and the walls are connected to the layout.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original essay about urban history.

Many medieval towns were built within defensive walls, and their streets are often narrow and winding. A historian notes that straighter, wider streets appeared in towns that expanded outside the walls once the threat of attack had lessened. This pattern suggests that the layout of the earlier streets
rw2h.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: was designed to make travel across the town faster.
was imposed by the same architects who built the later streets.
was shaped, at least in part, by the need for defence.
had little to do with the position of the walls.

rw2h.why: Dense cordgrass raised the surface in step with sea level while thin cover let the marsh drown, so restoring grass should help marshes survive. The text gives no support for sinking or for calm seas making grass unnecessary.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original science article.

A team studying a coastal marsh found that where cordgrass grew densely, the marsh surface rose by several millimetres a year, keeping pace with sea level. Where grass cover was thin, the surface barely rose, and the marsh was gradually drowned. The researchers conclude that restoring cordgrass is likely to
rw2h.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: cause marshes to sink more quickly in the future.
help marshes survive sea-level rise by raising their surface.
make the marsh surface lower in areas of dense grass.
be unnecessary wherever the sea is calm.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • They were made between about 500 BCE and 500 CE.
  • For decades, researchers could identify about 300 figures.
  • In 2019, machine learning software helped find more than 140 previously unknown figures.
  • The new figures are mostly small and were probably meant to be seen from the ground.

Machine learning software was used in 2019 to study the Nazca Lines.
The Nazca Lines, which for decades were thought to contain about 300 figures, are now known to include more than 140 additional ones identified in 2019 with machine learning software.

rw2h.why: The audience wants the key result and its limit, and only the first choice gives both the success rate and the false alarms. The others give the method, a call for trials, or the success rate alone.
rw2h.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • A study tested a new method for detecting early heart disease.
  • The method uses a 10-minute scan of the heart's electrical activity.

  • It also flagged 12 percent of healthy adults as having disease.
  • The researchers say further trials are needed.

In a study of 2,000 adults, a 10-minute scan correctly identified 94 percent of those with heart disease, though it also wrongly flagged 12 percent of healthy adults.
The researchers who tested the scan say that further trials are needed.
A 10-minute scan correctly identified 94 percent of those with disease in a sample of 2,000 adults.

Some farmers plough their fields before planting, and others use no-till farming.
No-till farming reduces erosion and often requires more herbicide.
Ploughing loosens the soil, which is why some farmers do it before planting.
